readings.c3s1:
¶
'''thatching''' (thach′ing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''thatch'', ''v.''] 1. The act or process of applying thatch, as to a roof.—2. The fibrous material of which thatch is composed, as straw.

'''thatching-fork''' (thach′ing-fôrk), ''n.'' A fork with a long handle, by which the bundles of straw, or the like, for thatching are brought up to the roof. ''Gwilt.''

'''thatching-spade''' (thach′ing-spād), ''n.'' Same as ''thatching-fork.''

'''thatch-palm''' (thach′päm), ''n.'' One of various palms whose leaves are suitable for thatching, particularly in the West Indies the royal palmetto, ''Sabal umbraculifera'', and in Lord Howe's Island (Australia) ''Howea Forsteriana.'' See ''thatch'' and ''thatch-tree.''

'''thatch-rake''' (thach′rāk), ''n.'' A utensil for raking or combing straight the straw or other material used in thatching, consisting of a straight bar in which curved teeth or points are set. {{smaller|In heraldry it is represented with five or six such curved teeth toward one end, the other end being left free as if for use as a handle.}}

'''thatch-sparrow''' (thach′spar″ō), ''n.'' The common sparrow, ''Passer domesticus.'' Also ''thack-sparrow.'' See cut under ''Passer.'' [Local, Eng.]

'''thatch-tree''' (thach′trē), ''n.'' The cocorite and other thatch-palms.

'''thatchwood-work''' (thach′wu̇d-wėrk), ''n.'' In
readings.c3s2:
''hydraul. engin.'', a method of facing embankments exposed to the wash of waves or current with underbrush held in place by strong stakes and cross-pins. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''thatchy''' (thach′i), ''a.'' Of thatch; resembling thatch. Compare ''Spartina.''

'''thatte†''', ''pron.'' and ''conj.'' [ME., a fusion of ''that, the'': ''that'', conj., ''the'', conj.] That. ''Chaucer.''

'''thaught''' (thât), ''n.'' Same as ''thoft''<sup>1</sup>, ''thwart''<sup>2</sup>.

'''thaumasite''' (thâ′ma-sīt), ''n.'' [< Gr. θαυμάζειν, wonder, marvel (< θαῦμα, a wonderful thing, a wonder), + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A mineral occurring in massive forms of a dull-white color, consisting of the silicate, carbonate, and sulphate of calcium with water. The name has reference to its unusual composition.

'''thaumatogenist''' (thâ-ma-toj′e-nist), ''n.'' [< ''thaumatogen-y'' + ''-ist.''] One who supports or believes in thaumatogeny: opposed to ''nomogenist.'' ''Owen.'' [Rare.]

'''thaumatogeny''' (thâ-mạ-toj′e-ni), ''n.'' [< Gr. θαῦμα(τ-), a wonderful thing, a wonder, + -γένεια, < -γενής, producing: see ''-geny.''] The fact or the doctrine of the miraculous origin of life: opposed to ''nomogeny.'' [Rare.]

{{smaller block|Nomogeny or ''Thaumatogeny?''
{{right|''Owen'', Anat. of Vert., III. 814.}}}}

'''thaumatography''' (thâ-mạ-tog′rạ-fi), ''n.'' A description of the wonders of the natural world.

'''thaumatolatry''' (thâ-mạ-tol′ạ-tri), ''n.'' [< Gr. θαῦμα(τ-), a wonderful thing, + λατρεία, worship.] Excessive admiration for what is wonderful; admiration of what is miraculous. ''Imp.''

Dict. [Rare.]

'''thaumatrope''' (thâ′ma̤-trōp), ''n.'' [Irreg. for *''thaumatotrope'', < Gr. θαῦμα(τ-), a wonder, + τρόπος, a turning.] An optical apparatus dependent for its effects upon the persistence of retinal impressions. {{smaller|It consists of a cylinder or disk upon which is depicted a series of images representing periodic phases of the same picture. When the disk or cylinder is rapidly revolved, the image of one phase persists while the image of the next falls upon the retina; so that the object seems to go through a series of movements.}}

'''thaumaturge''' (thâ′ma̤-tėrj), ''n.'' [= F. ''thaumaturge'' = Sp. ''taumaturgo'', < ML. ''thaumaturgus'', < Gr. θαυματουργός, wonder-working, < θαῦμα(τ-), a wonder, + *ἔργειν, work: see ''work''.] A worker of miracles; a wonder-worker; one who deals in wonders or (alleged) supernatural works.

{{smaller block|He is right also in comparing the wonderful works of Mohammed (who, however, according to the repeated and emphatic declaration of the Koran, was by no means a ''thaumaturge'') with the Mosaic and Christian miracles.
{{right|''The Academy.''}}}}

'''thaumaturgi''', ''n.'' Plural of ''thaumaturgus''.

'''thaumaturgic''' (thâ-ma̤-tėr′jik), ''a.'' [< ''thaumaturg-y'' + ''-ic''.] Of or pertaining to miracles or wonders; having the characteristics of a miracle; miraculous; also, in contempt, magical.

'''thaumaturgics''' (thâ-mạ-tėr′jiks), ''n. pl.'' [Pl. of ''thaumaturgic'' (see ''-ics'').] Miraculous or marvelous acts; feats of magic or legerdemain.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|that|6267|thaumaturgics}}</noinclude>{{smaller block|Treat it kindly, ''that'' it may
Wish at least with us to stay.
{{right|''Cowley'', The Epicure, l. 9.}}}}

{{smaller block|The life-blood of the slain
Poured out where thousands die ''that'' one may reign.
{{right|''Bryant'', Christmas in 1875.}}}}

3. Introducing a result or consequence.

{{smaller block|The buerne, with his bare sword, bere hym to dethe,
''That'' he felle of his fole flat to the ground!
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 6451.}}}}

{{smaller block|I neuer heard the olde song of Percy and Duglas ''that'' I found not my heart mooued more then with a Trumpet.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie.}}}}

{{smaller block|Learning hath that wonderfull power in it selfe ''that'' it can soften and temper the most sterne and savage nature.
{{right|''Spenser'', State of Ireland.}}}}

{{smaller block|Is cheating grown so common among men,
And thrives so well here, ''that'' the gods endeavour
To practise it above?
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iv. 2.}}}}

{{smaller block|What have I done
Dishonestly in my whole life, name it,
''That'' you should put so base a business to me?
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, iii. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|I knew him to be so honest a man ''that'' I could not reject his proposal.
{{right|''Swift'', Gulliver's Travels, iii. 1.}}}}

4. Introducing a clause as the subject or object of the principal verb, or as a necessary complement to a statement made.

{{smaller block|'Tis a causeless fantasy,
And childish error, ''that'' they are afraid.
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 898.}}}}

{{smaller block|You gave consent ''that'', to defeat my brother,
I should take any course.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, iv. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|This is most certain, ''that'' the king was ever friendly to the Irish Papists.
{{right|''Milton'', Eikonoklastes, xii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The Naragansett men told us after ''that'' thirteen of the Pequods were killed, and forty wounded.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 233.}}}}

{{smaller block|I have shewed before ''that'' a mere possibility to the contrary can by no means hinder a thing from being highly credible.
{{right|''Bp. Wilkins.''}}}}

{{smaller block|It is a very common expression ''that'' such a one is very good-natured, but very passionate.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 438.}}}}

{{smaller block|The current opinion prevails ''that'' the study of Greek and Latin is loss of time.
{{right|''Swift'', Modern Education.}}}}

5. Seeing; since; inasmuch as.

{{smaller block|There is something in the wind, ''that'' we cannot get in.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iii. i. 69.}}}}

{{smaller block|Where is my father, ''that'' you come without him?
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, ii. 1.}}}}

6. Formerly often used after a preposition, introducing a noun-clause as the object of the preposition: as, ''before that'' he came, ''after that'' they had gone, etc., where at present the ''that'' is omitted and the preposition has become a conjunction; also, by mistaken analogy with such cases, ''that'' was occasionally added after real conjunctions, as ''when that, where that.''

{{smaller block|Go, litil bill, and say thoue were with me
This same day at myne vp-Ryssinge,
''Where that'' y be-sought god of merci
Tho to haue my souerein in his kepeing.
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 40.}}}}

{{smaller block|''After that'' things are set in order here,
We'll follow them.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., ii. 2. 32.}}}}

{{smaller block|Take my soul . . .
''Before that'' England give the French the foil.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 3. 23.}}}}

{{smaller block|What would you with her ''if that'' I be she?
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 4. 115.}} ''Since that'' my case is past the help of law.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1022.}}}}

{{smaller block|''When that'' mine eye is famish'd for a look.
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xlvii.}}}}

7. Sometimes used in place of another conjunction, in repetition. [A Gallicism.]

{{smaller block|Albeit Nature doth now and then . . . commit some errors, and ''that'' sometimes the things shee formeth haue too much, and sometimes too little, yet deliuereth she nothing broken or disseuered.
{{right|''Verstegan'', Restitution of Decayed Intelligence (ed. 1628), [p. 98.}}}}

8. Used elliptically to introduce a sentence or clause expressive of surprise, indignation, or some kindred emotion.

{{smaller block|''That'' a brother should
Be so perfidious! {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, i. 2. 67.}}}}

{{smaller block|O God, ''that'' men should put an enemy in their mouths to steal away their brains! {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 3. 291.}}}}

9. Used as an optative particle, or to introduce a phrase expressing a wish: would that: usually with ''O!''

{{smaller block|''O, that'' you bore
The mind that I do! {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, ii. 1. 267.}}}}

{{smaller block|This was the very first suit at law that ever I had with any creature, and ''O that'' it might be the last!
{{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, May 26, 1671.}}}}

{{smaller|'''For that†.''' See ''for.''—'''In that.''' See ''in''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Now that.''' See ''now.''—'''So that.''' See ''so''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Though that†.''' See ''though.''}}

'''that''' (ᴛ̵ʜat), ''adv.'' [< ''that, pron.'' or ''a.''; abbr. of such phrases as ''to that extent, to that degree.''] To that extent; to that degree; to such a degree; so: as, I did not go ''that'' far; I did not care ''that'' much about it: the comparison being with something previously said or implied, as in the preceding examples: used colloquially to express emphasis. {{smaller|A similar Scotch use of the word, following a negative, corresponds to the Latin ''ita'' (as in Cicero's ''non ita multi''): as, no ''that'' bad; nae ''that'' far awa'.}}

{{smaller block|Ye think my muse nae ''that'' ill-faurd.
{{right|''Skinner'', Misc. Poetry, p. 109. (''Jamieson.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|This was carried with ''that'' little noise that for a good space the vigilant Bishop was not awak'd with it.
{{right|''Bp. Hacket'', Abp. Williams, ii. 67. (''Davies.'')}}}}

{{smaller block|Death! To die! I owe ''that'' much
To what, at least, I was.
{{right|''Browning'', Paracelsus, iv.}}}}

{{smaller block|Women were there, . . . because Mr. Elsmere had been "''that'' good" to them that anything they could do to oblige him "they would, and welcome."
{{right|''Mrs. Humphry Ward'', Robert Elsmere, xlix.}}}}

'''thatch''' (thach), ''v.'' [Also dial. (and historically more orig.) ''thetch'', assibilated form of ''thack'', ''theck'', also ''theak'', ''theek'' (still in dial. use); < ME. ''thacchen'', ''thecchen'', < AS. ''theccan'' = OS. ''theccian'' = OFries. ''thekka'', ''dekka'' = D. ''dekken'' = MLG. ''decken'' = OHG. ''dachjan'', ''decchan'', MHG. G. ''decken'' = Icel. ''thekja'' = Sw. ''täcka'' = Dan. ''tække'', thatch, ''dække'', cover, = Goth. *''thakjan'', cover; associated with the noun, AS. ''thæc'', etc., a roof, thatch, etc. (see ''thatch'', ''n.''); = L. ''tegere'', cover, = Gr. *τέγειν, also, with initial σ-, στέγειν, cover. From the L. verb are ult. E. ''tect'', ''protect'', ''tegument'', ''integument'', ''tile''<sup>1</sup>, etc. From the D. form of the verb is E. ''deck'', ''v.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To cover with or as with thatch.

{{smaller block|O knowledge ill-inhabited, worse than Jove in a ''thatched'' house!
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 3. 10.}}}}

{{smaller block|Thro' the thick hair thet ''thatch'd'' their browes Their eyes upon me stared.
{{right|''Drayton'', Muse's Elysium, iv.}}}}

{{smaller block|They ''theekit'' it o'er wi' birk and brume,
They ''theekit'' it o'er wi' heather.
{{right|''Bessie Bell and Mary Gray'' (Child's Ballads, III. 127).}}}}

{{smaller block|That lofty Pile, where Senates dictate Law,
When Tatius reign'd, was poorly ''thatch'd'' with Straw.
{{right|''Congreve'', tr. of Ovid's Art of Love.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To thatch houses.

{{smaller block|And somme he tauȝte to tille, to dyche, and to ''thecche''.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xix. 232.}}}}

{{smaller block|To plough, to plant, to reap, to rake, to sowe,
To hedge, to ditch, to thrash, to ''thetch'', to mowe.
{{right|''Spenser'', Mother Hub. Tale, l. 264.}}}}

'''thatch''' (thach), ''n.'' [Assibilated form of ''thack'' (still in dial. use), < ME. ''thak'', pl. ''thakkes'', roof, thatch, < AS. ''thæc'' = D. ''dak'' = OHG. ''dah'', MHG. ''dach'', covering, cover, G. ''dach'', roof, = Icel. ''thak'' = Sw. ''tak'' = Dan. ''tag'', roof, akin to Gr. τέγος, roof, L. ''toga'', robe (‘covering’), ''tegula'', tile, ''tugurium'', a hut, etc. (from the root seen in ''tegere''), and (with initial ''s'') to Gr. στέγη, roof, Lith. ''stógas'', roof: see ''thatch'', ''v.''] '''1.''' The covering of a roof or the like, made of straw or rushes, and in tropical countries of cocoanut-leaves and other long and thick-growing palm-leaves. {{smaller|The material is laid upon the roof to the thickness of a foot or more in such manner that the fibers run in the direction which the rain-water should take, and are held in place by cords which secure the upper part of each bundle, or in some similar manner. Long strips of wood loaded with stones are also used to keep thatch in place, and to resist the action of wind.}}

{{smaller block|They would ever in houses of ''thacke''
Here lives lead, and weare but blacke.
{{right|''Isle of Ladies'', l. 1773.}}}}

{{smaller block|O, for honour of our land, Let us not hang like roping icicles
Upon our houses' ''thatch'', whiles a more frosty people
Sweat drops of gallant youth in our rich fields!
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iii. 5. 24.}}}}

2. One of the palms ''Calyptrogyne Swartzii'' and ''Copernicia tectorum'', whose leaves are used in thatching. See also specific names below, and ''thatch-palm''.—{{smaller|'''Big''' or '''bull thatch'''. Same as ''royal palmetto (a)'' (which see, under ''palmetto'').—'''Brickley thatch, brittle thatch, silver thatch'''. Same as ''silver-top palmetto'' (which see, under ''palmetto'').—'''Palmetto thatch'''. Same as ''silk-top palmetto'' (which see, under ''palmetto'').}}

'''thatched-head''' (thacht′hed), ''n.'' One whose hair is matted together: formerly applied contemptuously to an Irishman, from his thickly matted hair. See ''glib''<sup>2</sup>.

{{smaller block|Ere ye go, sirrah ''Thatch'd-head'', would'st not thou
Be whipp'd, and think it justice?
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Coxcomb, ii.}}}}

'''thatcher''' (thach′ėr), ''n.'' [Also dial. ''thacker'', ''theeker''; < ME. *''thacchere'', ''theker'', < AS. ''thecere'' (= D. ''dekker'' = OHG. ''dechari'', MHG. G. ''decker'' = Dan. ''tækker''), a thatcher, < ''theccan'', thatch: see ''thatch''.] One whose occupation is to thatch houses.

{{smaller block|You merit new employments daily;
Our ''thatcher'', ditcher, gard'ner, baily. {{right|''Swift.''}}}}

'''thatch-grass''' (thach′grȧs), ''n.'' Grass or grass-like plants used for thatching; specifically, ''Elegia deusta'' (''Restio Chondropetalum''), of the ''Restiaceæ'', found at the Cape of Good Hope.
